ruled_out.assertion: The dynamic UPDATE builder concatenates a client-supplied column name into SQL
ruled_out.killed_by: the column comes only from the map at postgres.go:140-147 and an unknown field hard-fails at line 154; every value is bound as $N.

ruled_out.assertion: ParseFilter interpolates the wire filter into the WHERE clause
ruled_out.killed_by: the column is looked up in filterableColumns (search.go:16-22), the operator comes from the fixed regex alternation at search.go:31, and the literal is always appended to args as a bound parameter.

ruled_out.assertion: Search ORDER BY takes a client-supplied sort expression
ruled_out.killed_by: orderBy is produced by ParseOrderBy, which maps through sortableColumns (search.go:24-29) and appends a literal ASC/DESC.

ruled_out.assertion: gRPC server reflection exposes the schema in production
ruled_out.killed_by: reflection.Register runs only when CATALOG_ENV == "dev"; the default is "prod".

ruled_out.assertion: The permit listing interpolates a raw sort key into ORDER BY
ruled_out.killed_by: the value is bounced through the PermitSort enum at line 57 and a non-member is rejected with 400 before the query is built.

ruled_out.assertion: Attachment storage keys allow path traversal out of the blob root
ruled_out.killed_by: BlobStore.resolve enforces ^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$, a length cap and an explicit '..' rejection on both put and get. (The separate putRestored path, which skips this, is reported as a low finding.)

ruled_out.assertion: The rate limiter can be evaded with a spoofed X-Forwarded-For
ruled_out.killed_by: the fallback identity uses request.peerAddress, not a client-supplied forwarding header. (The bearer-prefix bucket is a separate, reported issue.)

ruled_out.assertion: innerHTML on the rendered report notes is an XSS sink
ruled_out.killed_by: renderNotes escapes &, <, >, " and ' first (app.js:8-19) and only then applies the bold/italic/break substitutions, so no tag can survive into the markup; the mitigation works.

ruled_out.assertion: Embedded webviews inherit dangerous preferences
ruled_out.killed_by: the will-attach-webview handler deletes the preload and forces nodeIntegration false / contextIsolation true for every attached webview.

ruled_out.assertion: The SFTP client accepts unknown host keys, enabling a man-in-the-middle
ruled_out.killed_by: load_host_keys plus paramiko.RejectPolicy() - an unknown host key aborts the connection.

ruled_out.assertion: A partner-controlled filename traverses out of the inbox prefix
ruled_out.killed_by: os.path.basename(name) strips any directory component before the remote path is built, on both fetch_one and fetch_all.

ruled_out.assertion: post_batch concatenates row values into the INSERT statement
ruled_out.killed_by: executemany with %s placeholders and a tuple per row - fully parameterised. The injection lives only in the COPY path, which is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: Consul intentions contain a wildcard allow that dissolves segmentation
ruled_out.killed_by: the wildcard source is Action = "deny"; the file is deny-by-default with two explicit allows. Its weakness is that ledger-db is not in the mesh at all, which is reported as its own finding.

ruled_out.assertion: Job artifacts are downloaded without integrity verification
ruled_out.killed_by: both artifact blocks pin an explicit sha256 checksum option.

ruled_out.assertion: trustForwardHeader: true lets an internet client forge X-Fleet-Role / X-Fleet-Tenant at the gateway
ruled_out.killed_by: the forwardAuth authResponseHeaders list overwrites those three headers with the auth sidecar's answer on every request, so a client-supplied value does not survive to the upstream.

ruled_out.assertion: The CI deploy token can mount host volumes or write node/agent/operator state
ruled_out.killed_by: there is no host_volume block, and node/agent/operator/quota are all policy = "read". The escalation path that does exist runs through privileged Docker re-enabled by bootstrap-node.sh, which is reported.

ruled_out.assertion: Retrieval is not tenant-scoped, so one workspace can read another's chunks
ruled_out.killed_by: every query filters byProperty('workspaceId') (weaviate.ts:64, 82, 109) and the workspaceId always comes from ctx.session, never from user or model input - so search_corpus cannot cross a workspace.

ruled_out.assertion: An injected instruction can make the model disclose MODEL_TOKEN
ruled_out.killed_by: MODEL_TOKEN is only ever used as an outbound Authorization header; it never enters the message array the model sees.

ruled_out.assertion: A secret split across a chunk boundary escapes redaction
ruled_out.killed_by: chunkText overlaps chunks by 150 characters, so any token shorter than 150 characters appears intact in at least one chunk and is redacted there.

ruled_out.assertion: Session token comparison leaks a timing oracle
ruled_out.killed_by: tokens are randomBytes(32) and lookup is a hash-map get on the digest, not a byte-by-byte comparison; expiry is enforced on every lookup.

ruled_out.assertion: Staff session tokens are generated from a weak random source
ruled_out.killed_by: UInt8.random(in:) draws from Swift's system CSPRNG, and only the SHA256 digest is stored; bcrypt with an enforced $2 prefix guards the password path.

ruled_out.assertion: Disabling TLS to Postgres exposes credentials on the wire
ruled_out.killed_by: TLS is disabled only when the host is 127.0.0.1/localhost, which is the in-pod pgbouncer sidecar; any genuinely remote host still negotiates TLS.

ruled_out.assertion: alloc-node-exec in the sandbox namespace gives host command execution today
ruled_out.killed_by: no raw_exec driver is enabled anywhere in the tree - all three job specs use driver = "docker" - so the capability is latent. It is reported at low with that constraint stated, not dropped.

findings.title: Auth interceptor lets the client overwrite its own role via the x-catalog-role metadata header, escalating any session to admin
findings.class: Privilege escalation / authorization decision from untrusted input (CWE-807, CWE-269)
findings.impact: Threat-model A2 (authenticated low-privilege tenant user) becomes a full admin on demand: create items, update any item in the tenant, publish items to VISIBILITY_PUBLIC (server.go:87,122 -- the admin-only publish gate is defeated by the same header), and delete items (server.go:153, admin-only). Tenant scoping still holds on these writes because TenantID is taken from the session and never from the header (server.go:92-93, postgres.go:139-184), so the damage is destructive/integrity within the caller's own tenant rather than cross-tenant -- but it is complete: an unprivileged viewer can wipe the tenant's whole catalogue one DeleteItem at a time and publish arbitrary content.
findings.recommendation: Delete lines 67-69. The role must come only from the session row. If the console genuinely needs to act under a narrower role than the session grants, the header may only ever NARROW: store the granted role set on the session, and accept the header only when the requested value is a member of that set and is not wider than session.Role -- never as an unchecked assignment. Independently, stop forwarding x-catalog-role from the internet-facing gateway (see searched below).

triage.reason: Not caller misuse: the interceptor in this tree performs the overwrite itself on every request, and the RPCs whose guards it defeats are registered in this tree (main.go:65).
An authorization decision taken from an attacker-supplied header is a control failure, not header hygiene.
Single deterministic request; the override is an unconditional assignment on a non-empty header.
No safe construct is being nitpicked; the code replaces a trusted value with an untrusted one.

No mitigation is being invented around. I checked for the obvious one -- validating the header against the session's granted roles -- and the Session type has no such field, so there is nothing to bypass.
Not a DoS claim.
Intrinsic flaw in the interceptor, and it is on the live path for every unary RPC. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'APPLIES_IN_FAVOUR']

Verified: interceptor.go:39-49, 51-72, 94-100; server.go:76, 87, 114, 122, 153; postgres.go:254-274; gateway/http.go:23-30. grep for 'x-catalog-role' returns exactly interceptor.go:67. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'VERIFIED']

Ingress point cited: catalog-grpc-store/internal/server/interceptor.go:67 via metadataValue -> metadata.FromIncomingContext (interceptor.go:40); the same value can also enter from the public HTTP surface at internal/gateway/http.go:40-42. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'CITED']

scope.established_by: internal/server/interceptor.go:67-68 -- an unvalidated request header assigned over the session-derived Caller.Role that RequireRole (interceptor.go:94-100) is the only consumer of.

searched.for: a granted-roles list the header value could be validated against
searched.found: nothing -- Session has one scalar field Role string (line 258) filled from a single `role` column (line 265). There is no role set anywhere in the schema (postgres.go:16-36 defines items and create_receipts only), so no membership check is even possible as written.

searched.for: whether the public HTTP front door strips or allows a client-supplied X-Catalog-Role
searched.found: It ALLOWS it. forwardedPrefixes (line 23) includes the blanket prefix "x-catalog-", and strippedHeaders (lines 27-30) lists only x-catalog-tenant and x-catalog-subject -- x-catalog-role is absent, so any internet client's X-Catalog-Role header is copied verbatim onto the gRPC call at line 46. It buys the attacker nothing extra today only because the gateway exposes just GetItem and Search (http.go:123-126), neither of which consults Role; the escalation is taken directly against the gRPC port.

searched.looked_in: catalog-grpc-store/internal/server/interceptor.go:94-100 and every RequireRole/caller.Role site in server.go
searched.for: a second, session-derived authorization check that would survive the header override
searched.found: nothing -- all six authorization decisions (server.go:76, 87, 114, 122, 153 and RequireRole itself) read caller.Role, which is the mutated field. No handler re-reads the session or re-queries the DB.

findings.title: ExportItems runs with no authentication (only a unary interceptor is installed) and takes its tenant from the client-supplied x-catalog-tenant metadata header
findings.class: Missing authentication for critical function (CWE-306) / tenant isolation bypass via client-controlled identity (CWE-807)
findings.evidence:
1) Only a UNARY interceptor is registered -- cmd/catalogd/main.go:50-59:
   48  \tauth := &server.AuthInterceptor{Sessions: store.NewSessionStore(pg)}
   50  \tgrpcServer := grpc.NewServer(
   51  \t\tgrpc.Creds(creds),
   52  \t\tgrpc.UnaryInterceptor(auth.Unary),
   53  \t\tgrpc.MaxRecvMsgSize(8<<20),
grep over the whole tree for StreamInterceptor / ChainStreamInterceptor / StreamServerInterceptor returns nothing. AuthInterceptor exposes only Unary (interceptor.go:75) -- there is no stream method to register.

2) ExportItems is a SERVER-STREAMING RPC -- proto/catalog.proto:81:
   81  \trpc ExportItems(ExportRequest) returns (stream Item);
so grpc-go dispatches it through the stream path, and auth.Unary never executes for it. No bearer token is required, parsed or looked up.

3) The handler then treats the absence of a caller as a routine case -- internal/server/server.go:202-216:
  202  func (s *Service) ExportItems(req *catalogv1.ExportRequest, stream catalogv1.Catalog_ExportItemsServer) error {
  203  \tctx := stream.Context()
  204  \tcaller, _ := CallerFrom(ctx)
  206  \ttenantID := caller.TenantID
  207  \tif tenantID == "" {
  210  \t\ttenantID = metadataValue(ctx, "x-catalog-tenant")
  211  \t}
  212  \tif tenantID == "" {
  213  \t\treturn status.Error(codes.InvalidArgument, "tenant could not be determined")
  214  \t}
  216  \tquery := store.ExportQuery(tenantID, req.GetFilter(), req.GetOrderBy())
Line 204 discards the ok flag that every other handler checks (server.go:44-47, 72-75, 110-113, 149-152, 167-170 all return codes.Unauthenticated when it is false). With no interceptor, ok is always false and caller is the zero Caller, so TenantID is "" and line 210 reads the tenant straight off the wire.

Mechanism: an attacker opens a gRPC connection to the service, sends metadata `x-catalog-tenant: <victim tenant uuid>` and an empty ExportRequest, and receives that tenant's entire items table streamed row by row (postgres.go:232-243 emits every row). No token, no role, no session lookup is involved anywhere on this path. The tenant value is also interpolated unescaped into `tenant_id = '%s'` (search.go:111), so `x-catalog-tenant: 0' OR 'a'='a` dumps every tenant without needing to know any uuid.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client that can reach the gRPC listener (cmd/catalogd/main.go:71 binds CATALOG_GRPC_ADDR, default :8443 on all interfaces) streams out any named tenant's full catalogue -- id, tenant_id, sku, title, description, visibility, price_minor, currency, updated_at for every row -- and with the quote-break above, all tenants at once. This is the single largest data-exfiltration path in the tree, and it is also the reachability that makes the ExportQuery SQL injection pre-auth. Even under the most conservative reachability assumption (port only reachable from inside the network / to any authenticated tenant user, threat-model A2), it hands one tenant every other tenant's product data.
findings.recommendation: Add a stream interceptor: give AuthInterceptor a Stream method that runs the same resolve() and wraps the ServerStream with the caller-bearing context, and register it with grpc.StreamInterceptor(auth.Stream) alongside the unary one in main.go. In ExportItems, stop discarding the ok flag -- `caller, ok := CallerFrom(ctx); if !ok { return status.Error(codes.Unauthenticated, ...) }` like every other handler -- and delete the x-catalog-tenant fallback entirely: the tenant must come from the session. If the nightly scheduler needs to export on behalf of a tenant, give it a service session per tenant, or require an explicit admin role plus an audited tenant argument in ExportRequest.

triage.reason: No hypothetical caller involved: main.go in this tree is the only server construction site and it omits the stream interceptor; the handler in this tree reads the header.
This is a missing authentication check on a data-exporting RPC plus identity taken from an attacker-controlled header, not a missing security header or hygiene item.

Fully deterministic: gRPC's dispatch of streaming methods past a unary-only interceptor is documented behaviour, and the handler's own `if tenantID == ""` branch shows the unauthenticated case was anticipated.
Nothing here is a lint of an already-safe construct; there is no auth on this path at all.
No working mitigation is being explained away. The one adjacent mitigation (gateway header stripping) is acknowledged above and shown not to cover this RPC, rather than being hand-waved.
The claim is unauthorised bulk data read, not exhaustion of a resource.
Intrinsic gap in the auth wiring; it also happens to be live for a registered RPC. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'APPLIES_IN_FAVOUR']

Verified: main.go:50-59 (interceptor registration), interceptor.go:75-91 (Unary only, health exemption on line 81), server.go:202-216, proto/catalog.proto:81 (stream Item), gateway/http.go:27-30 and 123-126. grep for stream interceptors returns nothing. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'VERIFIED']

Ingress point cited: catalog-grpc-store/internal/server/server.go:210, metadataValue(ctx, "x-catalog-tenant") -- attacker-set gRPC metadata; the RPC itself is entered with no credential because of cmd/catalogd/main.go:52. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'CITED']

scope.established_by: cmd/catalogd/main.go:52 registers only grpc.UnaryInterceptor, leaving the streaming RPC declared at proto/catalog.proto:81 with no authentication; internal/server/server.go:204,210 then substitute a client metadata header for the missing identity.

searched.for: which RPCs the interceptor exempts, and whether a stream equivalent exists
searched.found: Unary exempts exactly one method -- line 81: if info.FullMethod == "/grpc.health.v1.Health/Check" { return handler(ctx, req) }. Every other UNARY RPC is authenticated. But the type has no Stream/WrapServerStream method at all, so streaming RPCs are not covered by anything.

searched.for: any stream-level auth wiring anywhere, including a chained middleware package
searched.found: nothing -- zero matches in all 9 files.

searched.for: a gateway guard that would stop a client from supplying x-catalog-tenant
searched.found: The gateway DOES strip it -- strippedHeaders = {"x-catalog-tenant": true, "x-catalog-subject": true} at http.go:27-30, dropped at http.go:36-38. That guard is real but irrelevant to this finding: the gateway exposes no export route (http.go:123-126 routes only /v1/items/, /v1/items:search, /healthz) and the gRPC listener at main.go:71 is reachable without passing through the gateway at all.

searched.for: an in-handler RequireRole or tenant-ownership check compensating for the missing interceptor
searched.found: nothing -- ExportItems is the only handler in the file that calls neither RequireRole nor the `if !ok { Unauthenticated }` guard.

findings.title: SQL injection in ExportQuery: ExportItems filter/order_by/tenant are string-interpolated into the streaming SELECT with no allowlist and no bound parameters
findings.evidence:
Ingress (attacker data enters): internal/server/server.go:216 passes the wire fields of ExportRequest straight into the query builder --
  202  func (s *Service) ExportItems(req *catalogv1.ExportRequest, stream catalogv1.Catalog_ExportItemsServer) error {
  216  \tquery := store.ExportQuery(tenantID, req.GetFilter(), req.GetOrderBy())
  217  \treturn s.Store.StreamQuery(ctx, query, func(row *store.Row) error {
ExportRequest.filter (field 1) and ExportRequest.order_by (field 2) are plain client strings -- proto/catalog.proto:61-64.

Builder, internal/store/search.go:98-114:
   98  func ExportQuery(tenantID, filter, orderBy string) string {
   99  \twhere := "TRUE"
  100  \tif strings.TrimSpace(filter) != "" {
  101  \t\twhere = filter
  102  \t}
  103  \torder := "updated_at DESC"
  104  \tif strings.TrimSpace(orderBy) != "" {
  105  \t\torder = orderBy
  106  \t}
  108  \treturn fmt.Sprintf(
  109  \t\t`SELECT id, tenant_id, sku, title, description, visibility, price_minor, currency, updated_at
  110  \t\t FROM items
  111  \t\t WHERE tenant_id = '%s' AND (%s)
  112  \t\t ORDER BY %s`,
  113  \t\ttenantID, where, order,
  114  \t)
All three %s verbs are raw concatenation: `filter` lands inside the WHERE parentheses, `orderBy` lands after ORDER BY, and `tenantID` lands inside a single-quoted literal (so a quote in the tenant value also breaks out -- and that value is itself client-supplied, see server.go:210).

Execution, internal/store/postgres.go:225-226 -- the string is executed with ZERO arguments, so nothing is ever bound:
  225  func (p *Postgres) StreamQuery(ctx context.Context, query string, emit func(*Row) error) error {
  226  \trows, err := p.pool.Query(ctx, query)

Mechanism: filter=`TRUE) OR (TRUE` yields `WHERE tenant_id = '<t>' AND (TRUE) OR (TRUE) ORDER BY updated_at DESC` -- the whole items table, every tenant, streamed back over the RPC. The 9 projected columns also accept a UNION ALL arm with casts, e.g. filter=`FALSE) UNION ALL SELECT gen_random_uuid(), tenant_id, subject, role, token_digest, 0::smallint, 0::bigint, 'GBP', expires_at FROM api_sessions--` reads the session table quoted at postgres.go:265-267 (subject, tenant_id, role, token_digest). pgx v5 uses the extended protocol here, so stacked statements (`; DROP ...`) do not run, but single-statement UNION/boolean injection and arbitrary sub-SELECTs do.

Contrast with the SAFE sibling path: Search calls ParseFilter/ParseOrderBy (server.go:180-187), which allowlist the column and bind every literal (search.go:54-69). ExportItems calls neither.
findings.impact: Full read of the items table across every tenant, plus arbitrary single-statement SELECT against anything the catalog DB role can reach -- including api_sessions (subject, tenant_id, role, token_digest) which is the bearer-token table. Because ExportItems is a server-streaming RPC and no stream interceptor is installed (cmd/catalogd/main.go:50-59), this injection is reachable with no bearer token at all: an unauthenticated client that can open a gRPC connection to :8443 gets it. The stolen token_digests are sha256 of the bearer token (postgres.go:262,276-279) so they are not directly replayable, but the tenant/role/subject mapping and the entire catalogue (SKUs, titles, descriptions, prices) are read outright.
findings.recommendation: Route ExportItems through the same parser the Search path already uses: parsed, err := store.ParseFilter(req.GetFilter(), 1) and store.ParseOrderBy(req.GetOrderBy()), then build the export statement as `WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND (<parsed.SQL>) ORDER BY <allowlisted column+direction>` and pass tenantID plus parsed.Args to pool.Query. If the streaming path genuinely cannot hold bound parameters, keep the parser and interpolate ONLY the allowlisted column names and quote literals with a real escaping routine; never the raw wire strings. Delete ExportQuery's raw-string signature so the unsafe shape cannot be reintroduced.

triage.reason: Not hypothetical caller misuse: the unsafe call is present in this tree at server.go:216, and its arguments are proto wire fields, not values a hypothetical future caller might supply.
This is an injected predicate that changes which rows the database returns, not a missing header or hygiene nit.
Deterministic and reproducible: one gRPC ExportItems call with filter='TRUE) OR (TRUE' produces a valid statement every time; no race, no timing, no environment-specific condition.

This is the opposite of the pedantic case: the parameterised path exists (ParseFilter/ParseOrderBy + pool.Query(ctx, query, args...) at postgres.go:203) and this site deliberately bypasses it with fmt.Sprintf and a zero-arg Query.
No mitigation is being argued around -- ExportQuery has no escaping, quoting or allowlist to bypass. The allowlists that do exist are on a different function.
The impact claimed is data disclosure via injected predicates, not resource exhaustion.
The construct is intrinsically unsafe regardless of caller; it is also actually called at server.go:216. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'APPLIES_IN_FAVOUR']

Verified by reading the files: search.go:98-114 (ExportQuery), server.go:216 (call), postgres.go:225-226 (execution), proto/catalog.proto:61-64 (ExportRequest fields), search.go:16-29 (allowlists). grep confirms ExportQuery has exactly one caller. [normalised from reviewer verdict 'VERIFIED']
Ingress point cited: catalog-grpc-store/internal/server/server.go:216, req.GetFilter()/req.GetOrderBy() from ExportRequest (proto/catalog.proto:61-64). [normalised from reviewer verdict 'CITED']

scope.established_by: internal/store/search.go:108-114 -- fmt.Sprintf builds the whole predicate and sort from client strings, and internal/store/postgres.go:226 executes it with no argument list.

searched.for: a column allowlist applied to the export filter/order_by
searched.found: Both allowlists exist -- filterableColumns = {sku, currency, visibility, price_minor, title} and sortableColumns = {sku, title, price_minor, updated_at} -- but they are consulted ONLY by ParseFilter (search.go:54) and ParseOrderBy (search.go:82). ExportQuery (search.go:98) references neither map. Nothing narrows the export path.

searched.for: validation/sanitisation of req.GetFilter()/req.GetOrderBy() before the builder
searched.found: nothing -- the handler does no parsing at all; it only resolves a tenant id and calls ExportQuery on line 216.

searched.for: a variadic args parameter or any late binding that would parameterise the interpolated fragments
searched.found: nothing -- the signature is StreamQuery(ctx, query string, emit func(*Row) error) and line 226 is p.pool.Query(ctx, query) with no args. The doc comment on line 224 calls it a 'prepared statement', which it is not.

searched.for: whether the HTTP front door narrows exposure of the export RPC
searched.found: The gateway only routes /v1/items/, /v1/items:search and /healthz -- no export route. This does not narrow anything: cmd/catalogd/main.go:71 listens for gRPC directly on CATALOG_GRPC_ADDR (default :8443, all interfaces), which is the reachable surface for this RPC.

findings.title: Crawled document text is concatenated into the system prompt and the model's unvalidated tool arguments drive an outbound email sink (share_document)
findings.impact: Anyone who can place text on one of the four allowlisted documentation hosts (threat-model actor A4 - e.g. a partner-portal page, a comment/UGC area, a doc a partner uploads) gets to issue instructions that the model treats as house rules, because the passage lands inside the same system message as HOUSE_RULES. The reachable side effect is share_document: the injected text picks BOTH the recipient address and the note body, so the agent will POST to the internal notifier asking it to email an arbitrary external address, with up to a full model turn of free text in `note`. That text is generated from everything already in the model's window - the retrieved corpus passages of that workspace, the prior thread history, and the workspaceId/plan disclosed at prompt.ts:33-34 - which makes it a working exfiltration channel out of the tenant's corpus to an attacker mailbox, dressed up as a legitimate 'document share' from the product. Separately, `documentId` (tools.ts:100) is passed through with no check that the document belongs to ctx.session.workspaceId, so the app itself contributes no ownership constraint on what is being shared.
findings.recommendation: (1) Stop putting retrieved text in the system role: pass the corpus as a separate non-authoritative message (or a user-role block) with explicit fencing and a standing rule that content inside it is data, never instructions. jobs/telemetry-agent.nomad.hcl:
   4:  type        = "system"        <- runs on every client
   2:  datacenters = ["dc1", "dc2"]
  46:        mount {
  47:          type     = "bind"
  48:          source   = "/var/lib/nomad/alloc"
  49:          target   = "/var/lib/nomad/alloc"
  50:          readonly = true
  51:        }
The mount is the entire alloc root, not the log subtree the pipeline actually consumes. config/vector.toml only ever reads logs:
   5:include = ["/var/lib/nomad/alloc/*/alloc/logs/*.stdout.*", "/var/lib/nomad/alloc/*/alloc/logs/*.stderr.*"]
  10:include = ["/var/lib/nomad/alloc/*/traefik/local/access.log"]
but /var/lib/nomad/alloc/<alloc>/<task>/secrets is under the same root, and that is exactly where the other jobs render Vault material:
  jobs/ledger-db.nomad.hcl:65:        destination = "secrets/pg.env"
  jobs/ledger-db.nomad.hcl:69:POSTGRES_PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.superuser_password }}
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:67:        destination = "secrets/tls.env"
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:69:        perms       = "0644"
The edge-gateway spec even states the assumption this mount breaks:
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:65:      # Rendered into the task's private tmpfs; only this task can read it.
That claim holds only while nothing else can see the alloc tree. findings.impact: Compromise of the least-privileged component in the fleet - a log shipper that parses attacker-influenced data (gateway access logs from the internet-facing Traefik, plus every task's stdout/stderr) - converts directly into every Vault secret rendered on that node. telemetry-agent is a system job across dc1 and dc2, so this holds on the node running ledger-db (dc1, meta.storage_tier=nvme): reading /var/lib/nomad/alloc/*/postgres/secrets/pg.env yields POSTGRES_PASSWORD for the ledger superuser ledger_admin, which combined with Postgres being published on the host network at a static 5432 is immediate full control of the ledger database.   17:# Developer clusters run behind a self-signed CA that the runner image does not
  18:# carry, so certificate checking is relaxed outside the live fleet.

  21:fi

  13:cat >/etc/fleet/env <<EOF
  14:FLEET_ENV=${FLEET_ENV}
and render-secrets.sh sources exactly that file at line 10 ('. /etc/fleet/env'). So the two reachable values are 'production' (from /etc/fleet/env) and 'staging' (the default at line 13). findings.title: Permit listing cache key omits the tenant, so one council's permit list is served to every other council
findings.class: Cache Poisoning / Cross-Tenant Data Leak (Broken Access Control)
findings.evidence:
PermitController.list builds the cache key out of request-scoped inputs only, with no tenant component:

  38    func list(req: Request) async throws -> [PermitDTO] {
  39        let user = try req.auth.require(StaffUser.self)
  40        let status = try? req.query.get(String.self, at: "status")
  41        let page = max(1, (try? req.query.get(Int.self, at: "page")) ?? 1)
  42        let perPage = min(100, (try? req.query.get(Int.self, at: "perPage")) ?? 25)
  43
  44        let cacheKey = "permits:list:\(status ?? "any"):\(page):\(perPage)"
  45        if let hit = await ResponseCache.shared.value(for: cacheKey) {
  46            return hit
  47        }

and then stores the tenant-filtered rows under that same tenant-less key:

  61        let rows = try await sql.raw("""
  62            SELECT * FROM permits
  63            WHERE tenant_id = \(bind: user.tenantID)
  ...
  68        let payload = try rows.map { try $0.listProjection() }
  69        await ResponseCache.shared.store(payload, for: cacheKey)
  70        return payload

The store is a single process-wide actor - `static let shared = ResponseCache()` at Services/ResponseCache.swift:9 - keyed by a plain `[String: Entry]` (ResponseCache.swift:16) with a 45-second TTL (ResponseCache.swift:17). `user.tenantID`, which is the only thing separating councils, is used in the SQL at line 63 but never in the key at line 44.

Ingress: an authenticated request to GET /api/v1/permits (route registered at PermitController.swift:27, group at routes.swift:35-40). No unusual parameters are needed - the default key is literally `permits:list:any:1:25`, which every dashboard poll of every tenant computes.

Mechanism: tenant A's caseworker loads the dashboard, the payload for tenant A lands under `permits:list:any:1:25`; within the next 45 seconds any caseworker of tenant B hitting the same defaults gets tenant A's rows returned at line 46 before the SQL is ever reached. It is symmetric and continuous - the dashboards "poll every few seconds" per the class comment at ResponseCache.swift:4-7, so the shared slot is permanently hot.

Secondary defect visible in the same handler: the Fluent query built at lines 49-52 (including the `status` filter at line 51) is dead - the returned rows come from the raw SQL at 61-66, which has no status predicate. So `status` varies the cache key without varying the payload, meaning a `?status=refused` request can also be served, and can serve, an unfiltered cross-tenant list.
findings.impact: Any authenticated staff user of any tenant receives another council's permit list without touching an identifier or a parameter: reference, applicant name, applicant email, site address, summary, status and created_at for up to 100 permits per page (Models/Permit.swift:71-84 keeps all of those in the list projection; it only blanks internalReviewNotes and reviewerEmail). That is bulk applicant PII crossing the tenant boundary continuously, and it also flows the other way, so a low-privilege user in a throwaway tenant harvests other councils' data simply by polling. The same poisoning also lets a tenant's own view be replaced by foreign data, i.e. caseworkers act on the wrong council's records.
findings.recommendation: Include the tenant (and every other input that changes the result set, including the sort key) in the cache key: `"permits:list:\(user.tenantID):\(sort.rawValue):\(status ?? "any"):\(page):\(perPage)"`, and make `invalidate(prefix:)` tenant-aware accordingly. Separately, delete the dead Fluent query at lines 49-52 or apply the status filter in the raw SQL so the key and the payload agree.

triage.reason: The leak happens on the normal, in-tree call path of GET /api/v1/permits with default parameters - no caller misuse involved.
This is an actual authorization boundary being crossed with real data, not a hardening gap.
Deterministic in any multi-tenant deployment of this code: two tenants polling the same default listing within the 45s TTL is the documented normal usage (ResponseCache.swift:4-7).
No mitigation is being argued around; the tenant filter in SQL at line 63 is real but the cache short-circuits at line 46 before that SQL runs.
The claimed impact is data disclosure across tenants, not resource exhaustion.
Lines verified by reading PermitController.swift:38-70, ResponseCache.swift:8-48 and Models/Permit.swift:71-84.
The attacker controls the request that fills and reads the shared slot; ingress is GET /api/v1/permits, handler entry PermitController.swift:38, key construction PermitController.swift:44.

findings.title: /internal admin routes are registered with no authentication and no rate limiting on the same public listener
findings.class: Broken Access Control / Missing Authentication for Critical Function
findings.evidence:
routes.swift builds exactly one authenticated group and one bare group on the same `Application`:

  35    let api = app
  36        .grouped("api", "v1")
  37        .grouped(RateLimitMiddleware(limit: 120, window: 60))
  38        .grouped(BearerAuthMiddleware())
  39
  40    try api.register(collection: PermitController())
  41    try api.register(collection: AttachmentController())
  42
  43    // Case approval is driven by the caseworker desktop client, which talks to
  44    // the service over the council LAN rather than through the public edge.
  45    let internalRoutes = app.grouped("internal")
  46    try internalRoutes.register(collection: AdminController())

`app.grouped("internal")` adds a path prefix only. No `BearerAuthMiddleware()`, no `RateLimitMiddleware`, and no address/host restriction is attached anywhere. AdminController's four handlers confirm it: none of them calls `req.auth.require(StaffUser.self)` (grep over the whole tree shows `auth.require` only in PermitController lines 39/74/89/108/131 and AttachmentController lines 79/90/109/128 - never in AdminController). So every handler runs for an anonymous caller:

  AdminController.swift:23  routes.post("permits", ":permitID", "approve", use: approve)
  AdminController.swift:24  routes.get("permits", "export", use: exportAll)
  AdminController.swift:25  routes.post("attachments", "import", use: importAttachments)
  AdminController.swift:26  routes.get("sessions", "active", use: activeSessions)

Ingress point: the HTTP request line itself, dispatched by Vapor's router from routes.swift:45-46; the same server socket configured at configure.swift:8-9 serves both trees, and configure.swift never binds a second listener or restricts a hostname. The "council LAN" claim at routes.swift:43-44 is a comment with nothing implementing it.

Fully reproducible chain with no ID guessing: an ordinary staff user calls GET /api/v1/permits (PermitController.swift:38) which returns each permit's `id` (Permit.listProjection, Models/Permit.swift:71-84), then calls POST /internal/permits/<id>/approve with NO Authorization header at all and a body {"decision":"approved","reviewerEmail":"...","notes":"..."} - AdminController.swift:29-46 writes status, reviewerEmail and internalReviewNotes and saves.
findings.impact: Anonymous internet clients get the council's privileged case-management surface: (1) set a statutory planning permit to approved/refused/withdrawn and stamp arbitrary reviewerEmail and internal_review_notes onto it (AdminController.swift:40-43), i.e. forge a planning decision and its audit trail; (2) dump every permit of any tenant as CSV via GET /internal/permits/export?tenant=<uuid> including applicant name, site address and reviewer (AdminController.swift:48-77); (3) insert arbitrary attachment index rows on any permit (AdminController.swift:82-96); (4) read the live staff session count (AdminController.swift:98-104). Because there is no rate limit on this group either, all of it is scriptable at full speed. The write endpoints are also plain CSRF targets - no token, no origin check - so any web page a council employee visits can drive the approve endpoint from inside the LAN.
findings.recommendation: Attach authentication and authorization to the group, e.g. `let internalRoutes = app.grouped("internal").grouped(RateLimitMiddleware(...)).grouped(BearerAuthMiddleware()).grouped(RequireRoleMiddleware(.approver))`, and additionally bind these routes to a separate internal listener or enforce a source-network guard if LAN-only is really the intent. Do not rely on a path prefix or a comment as a trust boundary.

triage.reason: This is not caller misuse: the exposure is created by the registration in this tree at routes.swift:45-46, not by a hypothetical consumer calling an API wrongly.
This is a missing authentication control on state-changing endpoints, not a missing hardening header or defence-in-depth nicety.

Reproducible against any deployment of this code as written: the same listener serves /api/v1 and /internal, so any client that can reach the API can reach the admin routes. No exotic environment is assumed.
No mitigation is being argued around - there is literally no auth middleware, host check or role check on this path; I looked in routes.swift, configure.swift and the controller itself.
The impact claimed is unauthorized state change and data disclosure, not resource exhaustion.
All cited lines verified by reading the files: routes.swift:35-46, AdminController.swift:21-104, PermitController.swift:38, Models/Permit.swift:71-84.

Attacker control is the raw HTTP request; ingress is Vapor route dispatch established at routes.swift:45-46, with body decoding at AdminController.swift:36 and query input at AdminController.swift:49.

findings.title: vector.toml redaction covers only one structured shape, while the raw stdout/stderr of every task on every node is forwarded verbatim to the shared log bucket
findings.evidence:
The file states a guarantee:
  20:# Credentials must never reach the shared log bucket: the bearer token and any
  21:# Set-Cookie the upstream emitted are dropped before anything is forwarded.
  22:[transforms.redact]
  24:inputs = ["parse_access", "nomad_alloc_logs"]
  26:if exists(.request.headers.authorization) {
  27:  .request.headers.authorization = "[redacted]"
  28:}
  29:if exists(.response.headers."set-cookie") {
  30:  .response.headers."set-cookie" = "[redacted]"
  31:}
The transform has two inputs and only one of them can ever match. 'nomad_alloc_logs' is the raw container log stream:
   3:[sources.nomad_alloc_logs]
   4:type    = "file"
   5:include = ["/var/lib/nomad/alloc/*/alloc/logs/*.stdout.*", "/var/lib/nomad/alloc/*/alloc/logs/*.stderr.*"]
Those events are unparsed lines carrying the text in .message - they are never run through parse_access (which only takes 'gateway_access', line 14), so .request.headers.authorization never exists on them and both conditionals are no-ops. Every line every task writes to stdout/stderr on every node flows unmodified into:
  39:[sinks.log_bucket]
  41:inputs = ["sample_health"]
  42:bucket = "fleet-platform-logs"
  44:key_prefix = "raw/%Y/%m/%d/"
The other input is equally hollow, from the opposite direction: the gateway is configured to drop headers at source -
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:58:          "--accesslog.fields.headers.defaultmode=drop",
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:59:          "--accesslog.fields.headers.names.X-Fleet-Tenant=keep",
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:60:          "--accesslog.fields.headers.names.X-Fleet-Subject=keep",
so Authorization is not in the access log either, while the two headers that ARE kept and shipped are the resolved tenant and subject identity - which the redaction stage does not mention at all. Traefik's RequestPath field, which the filter at line 37 reads and the sink forwards, carries the raw query string, so any credential passed as a URL parameter reaches the bucket intact.
findings.impact: The comment is the control everyone downstream will trust, and it does not describe the pipeline's behaviour. The stream with the widest reach - stdout/stderr of every allocation in dc1 and dc2, which is where applications actually print tokens, connection strings and stack traces - has no redaction applied at any stage; it is written to a shared S3 bucket under key_prefix 'raw/', i.e. a location whose readership is broader than any single service's secret. Meanwhile the tenant and subject identifiers of every authenticated request to the internet-facing licensing API are exported to that same bucket as a matter of design. Anyone with read access to fleet-platform-logs inherits whatever the fleet's applications happen to log, and no code in this pipeline is trying to stop it.

Decide explicitly whether X-Fleet-Subject/X-Fleet-Tenant belong in a shared bucket and pseudonymise them if not. Then correct the comment at lines 20-21 to state what is actually covered.

The wiring is fully determined by the inputs= lists in the file; the gap does not depend on what any application happens to log - only the size of the consequence does, which is why confidence is 'probable' rather than 'confirmed'.
The gateway-side header drop is a real control and is credited explicitly in narrowed_by; the finding is about the alloc-log path it does not cover.

findings.title: ledger-db runs on the host network with a static 5432 and no Connect sidecar, so the Consul intentions protecting it cannot apply
findings.evidence:
consul/intentions.hcl builds a deny-by-default mesh policy for exactly this service:
   6:Name = "ledger-db"
  21:  {
  22:    Name   = "edge-gateway"
  23:    Action = "deny"
  24:  },
  26:    Name   = "fleet-console"
  27:    Action = "deny"
  30:    Name   = "*"
  31:    Action = "deny"
Intentions only govern traffic that goes through the Connect mesh. ledger-db is not in it:
  jobs/ledger-db.nomad.hcl:17:    network {
  18:      mode = "host"
  20:      port "pg" {
  21:        static = 5432
  22:      }
  31:    service {
  32:      name = "ledger-db"
  33:      port = "pg"
  35:      check {          <- and no connect { sidecar_service {} }
  47:        network_mode = "host"
The other two services in this tree do register sidecars (edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:34-36, telemetry-agent.nomad.hcl:19-28), so the omission on ledger-db is the anomaly, not the house style. With mode="host" plus network_mode="host" and a static port, Postgres binds the node's own interfaces on 5432 (the official postgres image sets listen_addresses='*'), and there is no proxy in front to evaluate an intention against. The header comment at intentions.hcl:2-3 - 'anything not listed here cannot dial anything else' - is therefore false for the one destination the file is written to protect.

CALIBRATION: Researcher proposed high. Downgraded: the mesh intentions are genuinely void, but Postgres still requires the Vault-issued superuser password and runs with ssl=on, so this is a segmentation failure rather than direct access. It becomes high only in the chain with the telemetry alloc-dir mount, which is filed separately.
findings.impact: The explicit deny of edge-gateway -> ledger-db and fleet-console -> ledger-db is decorative. Any workload that can route to the node - the internet-facing edge-gateway allocation, any other task on the node, any host on the node network, and A5 with a foothold on any edge node in dc1 - dials <node-ip>:5432 directly and never touches the mesh. Authentication then falls to the Postgres password alone, and that password is retrievable through the alloc-directory mount on the same node (jobs/telemetry-agent.nomad.hcl:46-51 reading jobs/ledger-db.nomad.hcl:65-73) or via a fleet-admin Vault token (scripts/render-secrets.sh:31). Host networking also puts the database in the same netns as the host, so the host_volume at /srv/pgdata and the socket are colocated with any privileged workload the bootstrap override permits.
findings.recommendation: Put ledger-db in the mesh: bridge mode, a connect { sidecar_service {} } stanza, and consumers reaching it through Connect upstreams so the intentions in consul/intentions.hcl actually adjudicate. If host networking is genuinely required for the WAL shipper and pgBackRest, then the intentions file is not the control - bind Postgres to a specific interface, add host firewall rules for 5432, and stop documenting mesh deny as the segmentation for this service.

findings.title: AppRole secret_id and role_id are passed as command-line arguments, exposing them in the process list on the CI runner
findings.evidence:
33:ROLE_ID="$(vault read -field=role_id "auth/approle/role/${ROLE}/role-id")"
  34:SECRET_ID="$(vault write -f -field=secret_id "auth/approle/role/${ROLE}/secret-id")"
  35:
  36:VAULT_TOKEN="$(vault write -field=token auth/approle/login \
  37:  role_id="$ROLE_ID" secret_id="$SECRET_ID")"
Both halves of the AppRole credential appear in argv of the `vault` process at line 36-37, so any local reader of /proc sees them for the lifetime of the call. Vault's own guidance is to supply these via stdin or an env var precisely because argv is world-readable. The tokens the script then produces are exported (38, 41) into the deploy environment, so they are additionally readable from /proc/<pid>/environ of every subsequent pipeline step.
findings.impact: A5 is defined as an attacker with a foothold on the CI runner - this is directly that attacker's cheapest win. A co-tenant process, a sibling pipeline job, or any compromised build step polling `ps` during a deploy captures role_id + secret_id and can mint Vault tokens for that role independently of the pipeline, outliving the deploy. When the job name misses the JOB_ROLES map (line 31) the role captured is fleet-admin. Nothing in the tree limits secret_id_num_uses or secret_id_ttl, so the captured pair is not necessarily single-use.
findings.recommendation: Keep the credential out of argv: `vault write -field=token auth/approle/login role_id=@- secret_id=@-` style stdin input, or set VAULT_ROLE_ID/VAULT_SECRET_ID and use a login helper that reads them from the environment. Better, use response-wrapped secret_ids with a short wrap TTL so an intercepted value is single-use and detectably consumed, and set secret_id_num_uses=1 on the roles.

findings.title: Attachment import endpoint mass-assigns client-supplied storage_key, permit_id and content_type, allowing forged attachment rows and HTML served inline from the API origin
findings.class: Mass Assignment -> Stored XSS / Broken Access Control
findings.evidence:
Every field of the persisted row comes straight off the wire, with no allowlist, no ownership check and no server-side key assignment:

  11    struct ImportedAttachment: Content {
  12        let permitID: UUID
  13        let displayName: String
  14        let contentType: String
  15        let byteSize: Int
  16        let storageKey: String
  17    }
  ...
  82    func importAttachments(req: Request) async throws -> [String: Int] {
  83        let rows = try req.content.decode([ImportedAttachment].self)
  84        var written = 0
  85        for row in rows {
  86            let attachment = Attachment()
  87            attachment.permitID = row.permitID
  88            attachment.displayName = row.displayName
  89            attachment.contentType = row.contentType
  90            attachment.byteSize = row.byteSize
  91            attachment.storageKey = row.storageKey
  92            try await attachment.save(on: req.db)

Two invariants that the rest of the tree relies on are broken here.

(1) storage_key is documented as server-assigned - Models/Permit.swift:29-30 says "Server-assigned. Uploads never influence where bytes land on disk" - and the legitimate upload path enforces it: `attachment.storageKey = UUID().uuidString + ".bin"` at PermitController.swift:154. Line 91 lets the client pick it, so an index row can be pointed at any blob already in the flat store (BlobStore.root, AttachmentController.swift:14, is one directory shared by all tenants).

(2) content_type is allowlisted on both real upload paths - `Self.allowedUploadTypes.contains(body.contentType)` at PermitController.swift:144 and AttachmentController.swift:113, against the set {application/pdf, image/png, image/jpeg, text/csv} at PermitController.swift:20-22. Line 89 has no such check, so an imported row can carry text/html. The download handler then echoes it as the response Content-Type with an inline disposition:

  AttachmentController.swift:100        headers.add(name: .contentType, value: attachment.contentType)
  AttachmentController.swift:101        headers.add(name: .contentDisposition, value: "inline")

Concrete chain, all in-tree: an authenticated staff user POSTs an attachment to a permit they own with contentType "image/png" and `data` set to arbitrary bytes - `data` is never sniffed, only counted (PermitController.swift:147) - and the response returns the whole Attachment including its storageKey (PermitController.swift:159; Attachment is a `Content` model with storage_key as a plain @Field, Models/Permit.swift:30). The same actor then POSTs /internal/attachments/import with permitID = that same permit, storageKey = the key just learned and contentType = "text/html". GET /api/v1/attachments/<new id>/content passes the tenant check (the permit really is theirs), reads the blob (AttachmentController.swift:98) and serves the attacker's HTML as text/html inline on the API's own origin.

Ingress: POST /internal/attachments/import, registered at AdminController.swift:25, body decoded at AdminController.swift:83. That route currently carries no authentication (routes.swift:45-46), so the import step needs no credential at all.
findings.impact: Two things an attacker gets in this tree. First, forged document index entries: rows can be attached to any permit id with any display name and byte size, injecting fake evidence into a permit file that then downloads and renders like a genuine attachment. Second, stored XSS on the API origin - arbitrary HTML/JS is served with Content-Type: text/html and Content-Disposition: inline to any staff user who opens the attachment, which in this design (bearer tokens issued to a browser client, routes.swift:9-13) means script running in a caseworker or supervisor session and able to drive every /api/v1 endpoint as that victim. Because storage_key is client-chosen, a row can also be pointed at any other blob in the shared store given its key, decoupling the tenant check from the bytes actually returned.
findings.recommendation: Never accept storage_key from a request: generate it server-side as the upload path does, or resolve it from a trusted manifest. Apply the same `allowedUploadTypes` allowlist to imported content types (and prefer serving attachments with a fixed safe Content-Type plus `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`). Verify permitID against the caller's tenant, and put the endpoint behind authentication and an import role.

triage.reason: The unvalidated assignment happens inside the HTTP handler itself; no assumption about a downstream caller is needed.
The core issue is mass assignment of a server-controlled key and an unvalidated content type on a persisted record, not a missing hardening header (the nosniff suggestion is only part of the fix).
Every step of the chain is an ordinary HTTP request against routes registered in this tree; no exotic environment is assumed.
Nothing here is a complaint about a standard library's safe behaviour - Fluent is used correctly; the defect is the application-level absence of an allowlist.
I did not claim to bypass BlobStore.resolve - I checked it and recorded that it works, and confined the finding to what remains possible with a well-formed key.
The impact is script execution and record forgery, not resource exhaustion.
Verified against AdminController.swift:11-17 and 82-96, AttachmentController.swift:14, 16-25, 98-103, PermitController.swift:20-23, 144-159 and Models/Permit.swift:23-36.

Attacker control is the JSON array decoded at AdminController.swift:83 (and the upload body at PermitController.swift:143 for the bytes); ingress routes are AdminController.swift:25 and PermitController.swift:32.

findings.evidence:
Three of the four handlers in this controller resolve the attachment's parent permit and compare its tenant to the caller's:

  78    func metadata(req: Request) async throws -> Attachment {
  79        let user = try req.auth.require(StaffUser.self)
  80        let attachment = try await load(req)
  81        guard let permit = try await Permit.find(attachment.permitID, on: req.db),
  82              permit.tenantID == user.tenantID

  84            throw Abort(.notFound)

(the same three lines appear in `download` at 92-94 and in `remove` at 130-132). `replaceContent` drops them and discards the authenticated principal entirely:

  108    func replaceContent(req: Request) async throws -> Attachment {
  109        _ = try req.auth.require(StaffUser.self)
  110        let attachment = try await load(req)
  111        let body = try req.content.decode(AttachmentReplace.self)
  112
  113        guard PermitController.allowedUploadTypes.contains(body.contentType) else {
  114            throw Abort(.unsupportedMediaType, reason: "content type not accepted")
  115        }
  116        guard body.data.count <= PermitController.maxUploadBytes else {
  117            throw Abort(.payloadTooLarge, reason: "attachment above 8MB")
  118        }
  119
  120        attachment.contentType = body.contentType
  121        attachment.byteSize = body.data.count
  122        try await attachment.save(on: req.db)
  123        try await BlobStore.put(key: attachment.storageKey, bytes: body.data)
  124        return attachment
  125    }

`load(req)` (lines 66-74) is a bare `Attachment.find(id, on: req.db)` with no tenant predicate - it is deliberately unscoped because every caller was supposed to scope it afterwards. The `_ =` at line 109 proves the omission is not a shadowed variable: the StaffUser is fetched and thrown away, so `user.tenantID` is never compared to anything. The two guards that remain (113, 116) are content-type and size checks, not authorization.

Ingress: PUT /api/v1/attachments/<attachmentID>/content, route registered at AttachmentController.swift:61 inside the group built at routes.swift:35-38, with the attachment id taken from the URL path at AttachmentController.swift:67 and the body decoded at line 111. The attacker needs only a valid session in any tenant.

CALIBRATION: Researcher proposed high. Downgraded: exploitation needs a foreign tenant's attachment UUIDv4 and I searched for an in-tree enumeration path (metadata/download/remove are all tenant-scoped; the CSV export returns permits, not attachment ids) and found none.
findings.impact: An authenticated staff user of tenant A replaces the stored bytes and the recorded content type of an attachment belonging to tenant B - the blob is overwritten in place at line 123 under the victim's own storage key, so the permit record still points at it and nothing marks it as changed. On a planning portal that means silently substituting the scanned evidence attached to another council's permit (site plans, certificates, objections) with attacker-chosen content, and the same call also lets any user tamper with documents on permits they merely happen to know the id of. Prerequisite, stated plainly: the attacker must know the target attachment's UUID - it is returned to whoever owns the attachment (PermitController.swift:159 returns the whole Attachment, AttachmentController.swift:86 returns it again) and travels in request URLs, so it is an identifier rather than a secret, but it is not enumerable from this tree.
findings.recommendation: Add the same guard the siblings use before mutating: resolve `Permit.find(attachment.permitID, on: req.db)` and require `permit.tenantID == user.tenantID`, aborting .notFound otherwise. Better, factor the scoped lookup into `load(_:)` so it takes the StaffUser and no handler can forget it.

A missing object-level authorization check on a mutating endpoint is a control failure, not defence-in-depth hygiene - the three sibling handlers show it is the intended control.
A single PUT with a valid session reproduces it; no unusual configuration or timing is required.
No mitigation is being explained away: I checked load(), the model, the route group and the middleware, and none of them enforces ownership.
The impact is unauthorized modification of another tenant's data, not exhaustion.

findings.title: The credential endpoint /auth/token sits outside the rate-limited group, leaving staff password guessing unthrottled

findings.title: Idempotency keys live in a global, tenant-less namespace and the collision error is returned verbatim to the client, disclosing another tenant's item UUID
findings.class: Cross-tenant information disclosure through error message / missing tenant scope on a shared key namespace (CWE-209, CWE-639)
findings.evidence:
The receipts table has no tenant column and the key is the primary key, so the namespace is global across all tenants -- internal/store/postgres.go:31-35:
   31  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS create_receipts (
   32      idempotency_key text PRIMARY KEY,
   33      item_id         uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES items (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
   34      created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
   35  );
The lookup has no tenant predicate and puts the other tenant's item id into the error -- postgres.go:102-110:
  102  \tif idempotencyKey != "" {
  103  \t\tvar existing string
  104  \t\terr := tx.QueryRow(ctx,
  105  \t\t\t`SELECT item_id::text FROM create_receipts WHERE idempotency_key = $1`,
  106  \t\t\tidempotencyKey,
  107  \t\t).Scan(&existing)
  108  \t\tif err == nil {
  109  \t\t\treturn nil, fmt.Errorf("idempotency key already used for item %s", existing)
  110  \t\t}
Compare every other query in the file, which all carry `tenant_id = $1` (postgres.go:90, 179, 184, 200). This one does not.

The error text is then handed to the client unmodified -- internal/server/server.go:102-105:
  102  \tstored, err := s.Store.CreateItem(ctx, row, req.GetIdempotencyKey())
  103  \tif err != nil {
  104  \t\treturn nil, status.Errorf(codes.AlreadyExists, "%v", err)
  105  \t}
Ingress: req.GetIdempotencyKey() -- CreateItemRequest.idempotency_key, proto/catalog.proto:38, described there as 'Optional client-supplied key'.

Mechanism: tenant B submits CreateItem with an idempotency_key that tenant A has used (client-chosen keys are commonly derived from order numbers, SKUs or dates, so they collide by construction across tenants). Line 105 finds A's receipt regardless of tenant, line 109 formats A's item uuid into the error, and server.go:104 returns it as the gRPC status message. The same `%v` passthrough also returns raw pgx/Postgres errors -- e.g. a unique violation on items_tenant_sku (postgres.go:29) with its constraint and table names. UpdateItem does the same at server.go:141 (`status.Errorf(codes.InvalidArgument, "%v", err)`).
findings.impact: An editor/admin in tenant B learns valid item UUIDs belonging to tenant A by probing plausible idempotency keys, and can also deny tenant A the use of any key it guesses (a squatted key permanently returns AlreadyExists for the rightful owner, since receipts are never scoped or expired). The uuids are the exact precondition for the id-keyed cache cross-tenant read in this same tree, so this is the disclosure primitive that feeds it. Rated low on its own: it requires a write-capable session and guessing a key the other tenant actually used, and the leak is one uuid per successful guess.
findings.recommendation: Add tenant_id to create_receipts, make the primary key (tenant_id, idempotency_key), and filter the SELECT at postgres.go:105 by the caller's tenant. Stop returning driver/internal error text to clients: at server.go:104 and 141, map known conditions to fixed messages (e.g. codes.AlreadyExists 'idempotency key already used' with no item id, codes.InvalidArgument 'item could not be updated') and log the detail server-side only.

triage.reason: Not hypothetical caller misuse: the unscoped query and the error formatting are both in this tree, and the handler that returns the text verbatim is in this tree.

The core of the finding is a missing tenant predicate on a shared table -- an isolation defect. The verbose-error part is reported only because it is what makes that defect observable, not on its own.
Deterministic: a colliding key produces the same disclosing error every time. I state the guessing precondition rather than claiming a reliable oracle for arbitrary uuids.
The query is parameterised and I am not faulting it for that; the fault is the absent tenant filter and the returned item_id.
The one real mitigation found (the gateway swallowing upstream errors) is recorded above and the finding is scoped to the gRPC path it does not cover, rather than being argued away.
Key squatting is mentioned as a side effect of the missing tenant scope, not claimed as a resource-exhaustion finding, and it is not the basis of the severity.

findings.title: Long-lived workspace API keys are verified by a single unsalted SHA-256 on an unauthenticated, unthrottled endpoint, with no entropy requirement and no failed-attempt accounting
findings.impact: An unauthenticated internet client (threat-model actor A1) can guess workspace API keys against auth.exchangeKey at full request rate with nothing counting the failures and nothing slowing the verification down - each guess costs the server one SHA-256. The same unsalted-and-fast digest is what protects the keys at rest in the map, so a memory disclosure or a heap dump yields digests that can be reversed offline for anything short of a high-entropy random key. findings.evidence:

  29:      service: fleet-console
  30:      middlewares:
  31:        - fleet-auth
  32:        - console-ratelimit
It shares the 'websecure' entrypoint with the public licensing routers (lines 8, 19), and that entrypoint is the internet-facing one:
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:16:    # This group terminates TLS for everything that arrives from the internet.
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:20:      port "https" {
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:21:        static = 443
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:22:        to     = 8443
  jobs/edge-gateway.nomad.hcl:54:          "--entrypoints.websecure.address=:8443",
Traefik routes on the Host header the client sends, not on DNS resolution, so the '.internal.' name is naming convention rather than a boundary: any internet client that opens TLS to the gateway and sends Host: console.fleet.internal.example is routed to the fleet-console backend. findings.title: BlobStore.putRestored writes to root.appendingPathComponent(key) with the key shape check deliberately skipped
findings.evidence:
The store has exactly one validator and one function that opts out of it. The validator:

  16    private static func resolve(_ key: String) throws -> URL {
  17        guard !key.isEmpty,
  18              key.count <= 80,
  19              key.range(of: "^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$", options: .regularExpression) != nil,
  20              !key.contains("..")
  21        else {
  22            throw BlobStoreError.badKey
  23        }
  24        return root.appendingPathComponent(key)
  25    }

is used by `put` (line 28) and `get` (line 34). `putRestored` joins the key onto the root directly:

  41    /// Used by the one-shot restore tool that streams a verified backup tarball
  42    /// straight back onto disk; the tarball index has already been checked so the
  43    /// per-entry shape check would only slow the restore down.
  44    static func putRestored(key: String, bytes: Data) async throws {
  45        let url = root.appendingPathComponent(key)
  46        try bytes.write(to: url, options: .atomic)
  47    }

A key such as "../../../etc/cron.d/x" or any absolute-looking segment therefore escapes `root` (AttachmentController.swift:14, default /var/lib/permits/blobs) and writes attacker-chosen bytes anywhere the service user can write. The rationale in the comment is the classic one - the caller is trusted to have validated - and it is exactly the property `resolve` exists to stop needing.

Honest scoping: I grepped the whole tree for `putRestored` and it has no callers - the only BlobStore calls are `put` at PermitController.swift:158 and AttachmentController.swift:123 and `get` at AttachmentController.swift:98. So there is no HTTP ingress for it in this tree and I am reporting it as a latent sink under the rule that intrinsic injection-class flaws are worth recording even when uncalled, not as an exploitable path today. The "restore tool" the comment refers to is not present in this repository.
findings.impact: Nothing today: no code path in this tree reaches it, so an attacker gets no capability from it as shipped. What it represents is a ready-made arbitrary-file-write primitive one caller away - the moment the described restore tool (or any migration/import job) is wired to it with entry names taken from a backup tarball or an operator-supplied manifest, a crafted entry name overwrites files outside the blob directory as the service account.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function or route it through `resolve(_:)` like its siblings; if a restore genuinely needs different rules, validate there too (reject keys containing a path separator or "..", and assert the resolved path is still under `root` via standardized-path prefix comparison) rather than skipping validation on the strength of an upstream promise.

findings.title: CORS falls open to every origin unless PORTAL_ENV is set to the exact string "production", using a different production signal than the rest of configure.swift
findings.evidence:
The allowed-origin decision is driven by an environment variable that defaults to a non-production value:

  46    let portalEnv = Environment.get("PORTAL_ENV") ?? "staging"
  47    let corsOrigin: CORSMiddleware.AllowOriginSetting =
  48        portalEnv == "production"
  49        ? .any(["https://permits.council.gov.example", "https://www.council.gov.example"])
  50        : .all
  ...
  55            configuration: .init(
  56                allowedOrigin: corsOrigin,
  57                allowedMethods: [.GET, .POST, .PUT, .PATCH, .DELETE, .OPTIONS],
  58                allowedHeaders: [.accept, .authorization, .contentType, .origin, .xRequestedWith],
  59                allowCredentials: true,

Two things make this fail open rather than fail closed. First, the default is `.all`: an unset or misspelled PORTAL_ENV, or a value like "prod", yields the permissive branch. Second, the same file already has a notion of production and it is a different one - line 70 uses Vapor's own `app.environment != .production` to decide whether to auto-migrate. A deployment started in Vapor's production environment but without PORTAL_ENV therefore skips auto-migration (correct) while serving wildcard CORS (not correct), and nothing reconciles the two signals.

The policy is broad in its own right: all mutating methods (line 57), the Authorization header explicitly allowed (line 58), credentials enabled (line 59) and a 600-second preflight cache (line 59-60).

What this concretely enables in this tree: the /internal admin routes require no authentication (routes.swift:45-46), so a permissive CORS policy lets any web page an employee visits both invoke and read them cross-origin - for example fetching GET /internal/permits/export?tenant=<uuid> and shipping the CSV to the attacker, or firing POST /internal/permits/<id>/approve. Confidence is marked probable rather than confirmed because the browser-visible consequence depends on the exact header Vapor emits for `.all`: if it is the literal wildcard, credentialed reads are still refused by the browser and the amplification is limited to the unauthenticated /internal routes; if the origin is mirrored as the comment at lines 43-45 describes ("we mirror whatever origin the browser sends"), the credentialed case opens up too. Under either reading, every origin is permitted whenever PORTAL_ENV is not exactly "production".
findings.impact: In any deployment where PORTAL_ENV is unset or misspelled - which is the default - arbitrary websites can script cross-origin requests to this API from a council employee's browser and read the responses of the endpoints that need no credential, notably the whole /internal admin surface. The severity is low on its own: the endpoints that hold tenant data behind bearer tokens are not directly readable by an origin that does not already hold a token, so this is an amplifier of the missing-authentication finding rather than an independent path to data.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: default to the pinned origin list and treat any unrecognised PORTAL_ENV as production, or derive the setting from Vapor's `app.environment` so the file has one notion of production. Drop `allowCredentials: true` unless a cookie-based flow actually needs it, and narrow `allowedMethods` to the verbs the browser client uses.

triage.reason: The policy is set in this tree's own configure() and applied to every response; no external caller assumption is involved.

CORS is adjacent to header hygiene, so I have kept the severity at low and stated the limitation explicitly; it is reported because it is an actively permissive access-control decision with a fail-open default, and because it has a concrete amplification against the unauthenticated /internal routes in this same tree. The permissive branch is the default path (PORTAL_ENV unset), not an exotic configuration.
I did not invent a bypass of the production pinning; I report the behaviour of the non-production branch, which is the default, and I state plainly what the browser still refuses.
No resource-exhaustion claim is made.
